newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO demands U.S. change its Mideast policy.
newsitem.headline: PLO demands U.S. change its Mideast policy.

text.p: PLO officials, frustrated with fruitless U.S. mediation efforts, said on Saturday the Clinton administration must rethink its Middle East policy if it is serious in seeking a breakthrough in Israel-PLO talks.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's adviser Ahmed Tibi charged that the administration, which has termed Jewish settlement an issue to be resolved between Israel and the PLO, was tacitly abandoning Washington's long-held rejection of settlement construction on occupied Palestinian land.
Tibi's comments followed the departure of U.S. special envoy Dennis Ross, who left the region overnight having failed to end a two-month impasse in PLO-Israeli peace talks.
Direct negotiations were suspended after Israel's decision to build a settlement in East Jerusalem.

In the West Bank town of Nablus some 2,000 supporters of the militant Islamic Hamas movement massed on Saturday in a "Rally for Jerusalem", denouncing the peace process in banners reading "No compromise and no peace".

Tibi told Reuters: "The U.S. administration must reconsider its Middle Eastern policies, especially concerning the PLO-Israeli track, if it is genuine in resolving the crisis ... because its policies so far have been a failure.
"It is time the U.S. changed its policy by focusing on the substance rather than on the process," he said.

Arafat, disappointed with Ross's performance during the nine-day mission, sent U.S. President Bill Clinton a letter on Thursday, urging him to upgrade the level of mediation and to involve himself personally in efforts to break the impasse.

The Palestinian leader bypassed Ross by sending the letter via the PLO representative in Washington. Arafat also snubbed the U.S. envoy by refusing to meet him on Thursday night, but agreed to see him on Friday before Ross left the region.
"The international community's position including that of the U.S. on settlements is that they are illegal," Tibi said.
"But the U.S. is now abandoning this position and adopting the Israeli position by hiding behind the pretext that settlements are a final-status issue."
Under the 1993 PLO-Israeli peace deal, settlements and Jerusalem are among volatile core issues left for "final status" talks to be completed by 1999.
The accord states that no side shall take unilateral actions that prejudge the outcome of permanent status talks, stalled since Israel's right-wing government took office in June.

Palestinians charge that Israel violated the accord in March by breaking ground on a settlement in East Jerusalem, which Israel occupied in 1967 and declared part of its capital in a claim unrecognised internationally. The PLO sees East Jerusalem as capital of a future Palestinian state.

Israel Radio said on Saturday Israel's Antiquities Authority had issued a stop-work order against a contractor building a road to the disputed settlement, after his bulldozers seriously damaged the remains of an ancient church at the site.
Officials were not immediately available for comment.

In another sign of an emerging credibility crisis with the United States, the Palestinian Authority accused Washington of abandoning its role in sponsoring the peace process by failing to press Israel to stop building settlements on Arab land.

"The U.S. failure to take quick, serious, responsible and practical action to put an end to the comprehensive Israeli encroachment on the peace process will be interpreted by the Palestinians and their national Authority as full abandonment by the U.S. administration of its role in sponsoring the peace process," the Authority said in a statement issued after its weekly meeting on Friday.
A U.S. official in Israel said in response that Ross was simply implementing U.S. foreign policy and making an honest, sincere effort to get the peace process back on track.
